name: Ranger Program
short_status: Nine spacecraft, 1961 to 1965: six straight failures, then Rangers 7, 8 and 9 returned the first US close-up images of the Moon before crashing into it. Program complete; last impact 24 Mar 1965 in Alphonsus crater.
tagline: NASA and JPL · United States · Programme · 1961 · The space race Success
stats: failed missions before the first success (Rangers 1 to 6)
images returned by the three successful Rangers (7, 8, 9)

facts.label: Program
facts.value: Nine uncrewed spacecraft launched 23 August 1961 to 21 March 1965, managed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory; total cost about $170 million

facts.label: Three block designs
facts.value: Block I (Rangers 1 to 2): Earth-orbit engineering test flights. Block II (Rangers 3 to 5): lunar probes carrying a TV camera and a balsa-wood-cushioned seismometer capsule to rough-land. Block III (Rangers 6 to 9): pure camera impactors with six TV cameras and no landing capsule

facts.label: Block I outcome
facts.value: Ranger 1 (23 Aug 1961) and Ranger 2 (18 Nov 1961) were stranded in low Earth orbit when the Agena B upper stage failed to restart; neither left for the Moon

facts.label: Ranger 4
facts.value: Launched 23 Apr 1962; on 26 Apr 1962 it became the first US spacecraft to reach the Moon, impacting the far side, but a central-computer/timer failure left it dead on arrival and it returned no images or data

facts.label: Ranger 6 failure
facts.value: Launched 30 Jan 1964; impacted Mare Tranquillitatis on target on 2 Feb 1964, but the TV system returned nothing; a review board blamed an arc-over after the cameras inadvertently switched on for about 67 seconds during booster separation

facts.label: Ranger 7
facts.value: Launched 28 Jul 1964, impacted 31 Jul 1964; returned 4,316 images of Mare Cognitum in its final 17 minutes, the first US close-up photographs of the Moon

facts.label: Mare Cognitum naming
facts.value: The impact area, between Mare Nubium and Oceanus Procellarum, was renamed Mare Cognitum, Latin for "the Known Sea," to mark the first lunar region seen close-up

facts.label: Ranger 8
facts.value: Launched 17 Feb 1965, impacted 20 Feb 1965; returned 7,137 images of Mare Tranquillitatis, near where Apollo 11 would land in 1969

facts.label: Ranger 9
facts.value: Launched 21 Mar 1965, impacted 24 Mar 1965 at 14:08 UT in Alphonsus crater; returned 5,814 images, with pictures converted for near-real-time broadcast on commercial television

facts.label: Ranger 7 impact crater
facts.value: The 14 m crater Ranger 7 dug was later identified in Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery at 10.634 S, 339.323 E (20.677 W) in Mare Cognitum

facts.label: Management
facts.value: James D. Burke was project manager for the failing Rangers 1 to 5; Harris M. Schurmeier took over and oversaw the three successful Block III missions

facts.label: Legacy
facts.value: The last three Rangers' photographs helped confirm the lunar surface would bear a lander's weight and fed Apollo landing-site planning, leading into the Surveyor soft-landers

timeline: Ranger 1 launches as a Block I engineering test flight but is stranded in low Earth orbit by an Agena B upper-stage failure; Ranger 2 meets the same fate on 18 Nov 1961
Ranger 3, the first Block II lunar probe, misses the Moon by roughly 36,800 km and enters solar orbit
Ranger 4 (launched 23 Apr) becomes the first US spacecraft to reach the Moon, hitting the far side, but a computer failure leaves it dead and it returns no data
Ranger 5 misses the Moon by about 725 km after a power failure and drifts into solar orbit; none of the Block II seismometer capsules ever reach the surface

Ranger 6 (launched 30 Jan), the first pure camera impactor, hits Mare Tranquillitatis on target, but its television system is dead; the failure comes just as NASA prepares to defend its budget to Congress
Ranger 7 (launched 28 Jul) redeems the program, returning 4,316 images of the region soon renamed Mare Cognitum in its last 17 minutes before impact
Ranger 8 (launched 17 Feb) sends back 7,137 images of Mare Tranquillitatis before impacting near the future Apollo 11 site
Ranger 9 (launched 21 Mar) crashes into Alphonsus crater at 14:08 UT after returning 5,814 images, some broadcast to American living rooms nearly as they arrived
